already carried by the imported finite piecewise $C^1$ boundary presentations
and by the compact $C^1$ surface measure cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ open and
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open interval. This definition fixes the
time-independent spatial test geometries of the integral form of the Maxwell
equations.

(a) [Volume test geometry] A **volume test geometry** in $\Omega$ is a pair
$(V,\nu_V)$ where $V\subseteq\Omega$ is a nonempty bounded open set with
$\overline V\subseteq\Omega$ and a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation
of its boundary ([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]), and
$\nu_V$ is the outward unit normal of that presentation off its edge set
([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]). The
**closed-surface flux** of a field $F$ continuous on a neighbourhood of
$\overline V$ is the finite face sum

$$\oint_{\partial V}F\cdot\nu_V\,dS:=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_V\,dS,$$

with the face surface integrals of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. For every closed
axis-parallel box $K=\prod_{i<3}[a_i,b_i]\subseteq\Omega$ with $a_i<b_i$, its
open interior $V=\prod_{i<3}(a_i,b_i)$ is a volume test geometry and
$\overline V=K$; its natural six-face presentation is the boundary of $K$, with
outward normals $\pm e_i$. The volume variable is $V$, while $K$ denotes its
compact closure. Each face is a degenerate three-dimensional box and hence has
$\lambda_3$-measure zero by
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]; their finite union
$K\setminus V$ is null. Thus for continuous $h$ on a neighbourhood of $K$,
$\int_Vh\,d\lambda_3=\int_Kh\,d\lambda_3$: the positive and negative integrals
over the null difference vanish by
[[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]] and
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

(b) [Patch test geometry] A **patch test geometry** in $\Omega$ is a regular
$C^2$ surface patch $(D,r)$ over a finite elementary Green region in the sense
of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]
([[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]],
[[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]]): $D\subseteq\mathbb
R^2$ is a finite elementary Green region, $r$ is of class $C^2$ on an open
neighbourhood of $D$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]),
$r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior of $D$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]) and
no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of $D$. Its
**induced boundary chain** $\partial S=r(\partial D)$ and its **circulation**
$\oint_{\partial S}F\cdot d\mathbf r$ for a field continuous on the image are
those of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]
([[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]); its
**oriented flux** of a field $F$ continuous on the image is

$$\int_SF\cdot n_S\,dS:=\int_D(F\circ r)\cdot(r_u\times r_v)\,dudv,$$

the scalar Riemann integral of the continuous integrand on the compact Jordan
parameter region, in the orientation induced by $r$
([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]). The pair $(D,r)$
is part of the data. Every affine graph patch $r(u,v)=(u,v,\varphi(u,v))$ over
an axis-parallel square $D=[c_1,c_1+\ell]\times[c_2,c_2+\ell]$ with $\ell>0$,
whose graph lies in $\Omega$ with $\varphi$ affine (for instance constant), and
more generally every affine regular patch over such a square, is a patch test
geometry: the square is a finite elementary Green region, and $r$ is smooth and
regular with $\varphi_u,\varphi_v$ constant.

(c) [Regularity convention] When an integral identity of this framework is
asserted for a volume test geometry $V$, respectively for a patch test geometry
$S$, with respect to a field $F$ of stated class $C^k$, it concerns fields
defined and of class $C^k$ on an open neighbourhood of $\overline V$ in
$\Omega$, respectively of the image $r[D]$ in $\Omega$; when the identity
involves a time derivative of a flux, the field is defined with the stated
regularity on a neighbourhood of that compact set times the compact time
interval of the assertion. No regularity away from these neighbourhoods is
asserted.

(d) [Conventions and scope] Test geometries are fixed spatial subsets of
$\Omega$ and carry no motion. A patch's orientation is the one induced by its
parametrization, and its induced boundary chain has the compatible orientation
of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]], so that the
classical Stokes theorem applies with a plus sign. The definition retains the
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the imported boundary and surface-measure
definitions; it asserts no differential equation, no physical law and no
existence of fields.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of the
imported piecewise $C^1$ boundary and surface-measure definitions
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; let
$E,B$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and $\rho,J$ source fields of
[[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$; and let $(V,\nu_V)$ and $(D,r)$ be the
volume and patch test geometries of [[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]]. Assume the
fields are jointly $C^1$ on $\Omega\times I$ and that the additional
derivatives appearing below exist and are continuous there; for instance $E,B$
jointly of class $C^2$ and $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$ is sufficient.

(a) [Differential implies integral] If the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, then for every
volume test geometry $(V,\nu_V)$ and every $t\in I$,

$$\oint_{\partial V}E(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int_V\rho(\cdot,t)\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \oint_{\partial V}B(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=0,$$

and for every patch test geometry $(D,r)$ the flux functions
$t\mapsto\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ and
$t\mapsto\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ are differentiable on $I$ and, for
every $t\in I$,

$$\oint_{\partial S}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS,\qquad \oint_{\partial S}B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\mu_0\int_SJ(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS+c^{-2}\frac{d}{dt}\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS.$$

(b) [Integral implies differential] Conversely, suppose the two volume
identities of (a) hold for every volume test geometry and every $t\in I$, and
that for every patch test geometry the two flux functions are differentiable
on $I$ and the two patch identities of (a) hold for every $t\in I$. Then the
four smooth-branch equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] hold pointwise on
$\Omega\times I$:

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

The equivalence is asserted for the exact class of test geometries of
[[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]], which contains the open interiors of all closed
axis-parallel boxes compactly contained in $\Omega$ and the affine square
patches; it is not a recovery from one selected volume or one selected patch,
and the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the time derivative of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] are the operators used.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) $E$ is a **polar vector** and $B$ an **axial vector** relative to the
orientation of the spatial basis; the changes of inertial description adopted
for this framework are proper and orientation preserving, so
orientation-reversing descriptions are not among them.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be piecewise-$C^1$. If $a=b$, define both line integrals below to be $0$. If $a<b$, choose an admissible partition $a=t_0<\cdots<t_m=b$ and a continuous derivative extension $v_i$ on each piece. Let $f$ be a continuous scalar field and $F$ a continuous vector field on a set containing the trace of $\gamma$. The **scalar line integral with respect to arc length** and the **vector-field line integral** are

$$\int_\gamma f\,ds:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}f(\gamma(t))\lVert v_i(t)\rVert_2\,dt,$$

$$\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt,$$

where the inner product is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The summands exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. Independence of the admissible partition is proved in [[lem-line-integrals-are-independent-of-the-piecewise-c1-partition]].

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Adopt as physical postulates of this framework, on the spacetime and particle
model of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and
[[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] and on the special-relativity particle
model [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]:

(i) [Test charge in a prescribed external field] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a
constant charge parameter ([[def-em-sources]]), $m>0$ an externally supplied
rest mass, $x:J\to A$ a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline with
four-velocity $U$, and let $F$ be a prescribed field of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph
of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle. Adopt the equation of
motion

$$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),$$

where $\Phi$ is the raised-index operator of the field at the event $x(\tau)$,
defined by $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$
([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]); equivalently
$m\,dU^\mu/d\tau=q\,F^{\mu\nu}U_\nu$. Here $dU/d\tau$ is the derivative of $U$
with respect to proper time, that is, the four-acceleration of the worldline
([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). The particle's own field
is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no
self-force.

(ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of
[[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated
matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density
$\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit
W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the
spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local
interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed
current alone.

(iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within
electromagnetism. The coupling is adopted for constant $q$ and $m>0$; no
magnetic-monopole coupling, no radiation reaction and no self-force are
included. In particular the nonrelativistic coordinate statement
$mr''=q(E+r'\times B)$ is not adopted as exact: the adopted statement is the
covariant one of clause (i), and any low-speed statement requires its own
approximation hypotheses and error bounds.

derivations.claim:
The circuit data of [F1] satisfy the hypotheses of [F3]: $r$ extends $C^2$ to a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ with the cross product nonzero on the interior, $v$ is single-valued of class $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set, and $B$ is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set because it is jointly $C^2$ on $\Omega\times I$ and $r(D\times I)\subseteq\Omega$ (indeed $B$ is $C^2$ there); and $\operatorname{div}B=0$ pointwise by [F9]. Hence $\Phi_B$ is differentiable on $I$ and [F1, F3, F6, F9]
$$\Phi_B'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r$$
for every $t\in I$, the boundary integral using the induced orientation of the patch boundary, which is the orientation of the path $\gamma_t$ of [F1] and [F2].

Fix $t\in J$. The frozen data $(D,r(\cdot,\cdot,t))$ is a patch test geometry of [F4]: $D$ is a finite elementary Green region, $r(\cdot,\cdot,t)$ is $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of $D$, its cross product is nonzero on the interior of $D$, and injectivity of $r(\cdot,t)$ on $D$ by [F1] implies that no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of $D$; its image $S(t)=r(D,t)$ is compact and contained in the open set $\Omega$. Moreover $E,B$ are jointly $C^2$ and $\rho,J$ are $C^1$, so the smooth branch hypothesis of [F5] holds by [F9], [F6] and [F8]. Applying the patch clause of [F5] to the fixed patch $(D,r(\cdot,\cdot,t))$ gives that the frozen-patch flux function $s\mapsto\int_{S(t)}B(\cdot,s)\cdot n\,dS$ is differentiable on $I$ with derivative at $s=t$ equal to $\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS$, and that [F1, F4, F5, F6, F8, F9]
$$\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS=-\oint_{\partial S(t)}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r,$$
the circulation being over the induced boundary chain of the patch, that is, over $\gamma_t$ with the orientation of [F1] and [F2].

At every $t\in J$ the line integral of the sum splits: for the piecewise $C^1$ closed path $\gamma_t$, the identity $\langle E+v\times B,d\mathbf r\rangle=\langle E,d\mathbf r\rangle+\langle v\times B,d\mathbf r\rangle$ holds pointwise along the path by additivity of the inner product [F11], so the definition [F13] and the Riemann-integral linearity [F12] applied to the finitely many arcs give $\oint_{\gamma_t}(E+v\times B)(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\oint_{\gamma_t}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r+\oint_{\gamma_t}(v\times B)(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r$, which is $\mathrm{emf}(t)$ by [F2]. Substituting the frozen-patch identity of step 1.2 into the first term, and then combining the two terms through the transport formula of step 1.1, yields [F2, F11, F12, F13, step 1.1, step 1.2]
$$\mathrm{emf}(t)=-\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS+\oint_{\gamma_t}(v\times B)(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\Phi_B'(t),$$
for every $t\in J$.

The frozen patch is a test geometry for every $t\in J$ (step 1.2), the fixed-patch Faraday identity holds (step 1.2), and the emf identity holds for every $t\in J$ (step 2.1); the flux formula of step 1.1 holds on all of $I$. The physical reading of the integrand as the force per unit charge on charges moving with the conductor material is the adopted coupling [F10], whose exact relativistic form is the covariant equation and whose nonrelativistic coordinate statement is not adopted as exact; the algebraic identity itself uses only [F1]-[F13]. The constants and units are those of [F6] and [F7]; the result asserts no fixed-loop formula for arbitrary moving loops, no field uniqueness and no statement about singular supports, and the no-singularity-crossing hypothesis is the containment of the swept set in the open region $\Omega$ on which the fields satisfy the stated regularity, where each image $S(t)$ is compact for $t\in I$ and the subinterval $J$ records the declared window. Countable Choice enters only through [A1] in the cited transport and integral-Maxwell suppliers.

boundaries.evidence: The claims quantify over $t$ in the compact subinterval $J$; if $J$ is empty the assertions are vacuous, and steps 1.1-2.1 apply pointwise to every nonempty case. The statement and proof assert no nonemptiness of $J$.

For $E=B=0$ and zero sources the smooth branch of [F9] holds; step 1.1 gives $\Phi_B\equiv0$ with $\Phi_B'\equiv0$, step 1.2 gives the frozen-patch Faraday identity $0=0$, and step 2.1 gives $\mathrm{emf}\equiv0=-\Phi_B'$.
No counting parameter occurs; the circuit has a single sheet $r$ and a single velocity field $v$, and step 1.1 applies the transport formula once and step 1.2 the Faraday clause once.

Rank failures are permitted on the boundary of $D$ by [F1] (condition on the interior only); step 1.2 uses injectivity of $r(\cdot,t)$ on $D$ exactly as [F1] supplies it, and the trace $C(t)$ may have corner points without changing the line-integral convention [F13].

$I$ is an open interval; the subinterval $J$ may be closed and no time derivative at the endpoints of $J$ is taken. Steps 1.2 and 2.1 evaluate all integrals at a fixed $t\in J$ over the compact patch, so included endpoints of $J$ need no one-sided derivative.

Countable Choice is inherited from the transport lemma [F3] and the integral-Maxwell theorem [F5], as the Statement records and step 3.1 repeats; no stronger choice principle is used in steps 1.1-2.1.
No if-and-only-if claim is made; step 2.1 proves the emf identity for every $t\in J$, and the physical reading of [F10] is explanatory.
There is no converse direction; the statement asserts the single identity $\mathrm{emf}(t)=-\Phi_B'(t)$ and no formula recovering a field from an emf.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be piecewise-$C^1$. If $a=b$, define both line integrals below to be $0$. If $a<b$, choose an admissible partition $a=t_0<\cdots<t_m=b$ and a continuous derivative extension $v_i$ on each piece. Let $f$ be a continuous scalar field and $F$ a continuous vector field on a set containing the trace of $\gamma$. The **scalar line integral with respect to arc length** and the **vector-field line integral** are

$$\int_\gamma f\,ds:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}f(\gamma(t))\lVert v_i(t)\rVert_2\,dt,$$

$$\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt,$$

where the inner product is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The summands exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. Independence of the admissible partition is proved in [[lem-line-integrals-are-independent-of-the-piecewise-c1-partition]].

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) $E$ is a **polar vector** and $B$ an **axial vector** relative to the
orientation of the spatial basis; the changes of inertial description adopted
for this framework are proper and orientation preserving, so
orientation-reversing descriptions are not among them.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let the laboratory region $\Omega\times I$ and its inertial chart, the field objects $E,B$ and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], with $c>0$; here $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ is a nonempty open set and $I$ is a nonempty open interval.

(a) [Moving material circuit] A **moving material circuit** on the laboratory region is the data $(D,r,v)$ specified as follows. $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a compact finite elementary Green region with its positive boundary chain ([[def-em-moving-patch]]); $r:D\times I\to\Omega$ extends to a $C^2$ map on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior of $D$ and $r(\cdot,t)$ injective on $D$ for every $t\in I$ (embedded material sheet); and $v$ is a $C^1$ vector field on a neighbourhood of the swept set $S=\bigcup_{t\in I}r(D\times\{t\})$ in $\Omega\times I$ satisfying the single-valued condition $v(r(u,w,t),t)=\partial_tr(u,w,t)$ for all $(u,w)\in D$ and all $t\in I$. In the notation of [[def-em-moving-patch]] the map $r$ is the swept moving patch and $v$ is its single-valued velocity; material points of the circuit are the images of the parameter points $(u,w)$.

(b) [Surface, boundary and flux] For $t\in I$ put $S(t):=r(D,t)$ and let
$$\gamma_t:=r(\cdot,t)|_{\partial D}$$
be the positive boundary chain of $D$ composed with $r(\cdot,t)$; its trace is the set $C(t):=r(\partial D,t)$, and $C(t)$ carries the boundary orientation induced by the positive orientation of $D$. For $B$ of class $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set, the **magnetic flux** of the circuit at time $t$ is the parametrized flux
$$\Phi_B(t):=\int_D\bigl\langle B(r(u,w,t),t),\,r_u(u,w,t)\times r_v(u,w,t)\bigr\rangle\,du\,dw$$
of [[def-em-moving-patch]]; its unit is the weber, $\mathrm{Wb}=\mathrm{T}\,\mathrm{m}^2$.

(c) [Electromotive force] For $E,B$ continuous on a neighbourhood of the swept set, the **electromotive force** (emf) of the circuit at time $t$ is the vector line integral over the oriented closed path $\gamma_t$
$$\mathrm{emf}(t):=\oint_{\gamma_t}\bigl\langle E(\cdot,t)+v(\cdot,t)\times B(\cdot,t),\,d\mathbf r\bigr\rangle$$
in the convention of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]], with the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; its unit is the volt, $1\,\mathrm V=1\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm s^{-3}\mathrm A^{-1}$. Under the framework's Lorentz coupling the integrand is the force per unit charge on a charge moving with the conductor material; the definition itself only names the line integral.

(d) [Scope and exclusions] The fields are assumed of the stated regularity on a neighbourhood of the swept set: circuits passing through a point charge, a curve or surface singularity, or any place where the fields fail to be of that regularity are excluded (no singularity crossings). When the emf is interpreted through the framework's relativistic Lorentz coupling, material speeds are required to be subluminal, $|v|<c$. The definition asserts no conservation law and no relation between $\mathrm{emf}$ and $\Phi_B'$; in particular the flux concerns the single field $B$ and the emf the pair $(E,B)$, and neither object is claimed independent of the chosen parametrization.

### Well-definedness and conventions

*The flux is well defined.* With $B$ and $r$ of the stated regularity, the integrand of (b) is continuous on the compact Jordan measurable set $D$, so the Riemann integral exists and coincides with the flux of the moving patch $(D,r,v)$ in [[def-em-moving-patch]]; the value is independent of any $C^2$ extension of $r$ by the conventions recorded there.

*The boundary path is a closed piecewise $C^1$ path.* The positive boundary chain of a finite elementary Green region is a finite concatenation of $C^1$ arcs ([[def-em-moving-patch]] and the boundary-orientation conventions cited there); composing each arc with the $C^2$ map $r(\cdot,t)$ gives a finite concatenation of $C^1$ arcs with matching one-sided endpoints and equal initial and terminal points, that is, a closed piecewise $C^1$ path in the sense of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]. Its trace is $C(t)\subseteq S$, and $E+v\times B$ is continuous on a neighbourhood of $S$, hence on the trace; the line integral of (c) is therefore defined and independent of the admissible partition of the path. The integral is unchanged by the chosen $C^2$ extension of $r$, because the path and the integrand depend only on the values of $r$ and $v$ on $D\times I$ and on the neighbourhood of $S$ recorded in the data; it depends on the orientation of $D$, as recorded in (b).

*The embedded sheet and its boundary.* Because $r(\cdot,t)$ is injective and continuous on the compact set $D$, each slice $S(t)=r(D,t)$ is an embedded sheet homeomorphic to $D$, and $r(\partial D,t)=\partial S(t)$ is its topological boundary; the parametrized path $\gamma_t$ therefore parametrizes the positively oriented boundary of $S(t)$ induced by the positive orientation of $D$, with the orientation fixed by the boundary chain as in (b). Rank failures on the boundary of the parameter region (seams) remain permitted, since $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ is required only on the interior.

*No physical assertion.* The definition introduces geometric data, a flux integral and an emf line integral, with the stated regularity, orientation and unit conventions. It asserts no field equations, no relation between $\mathrm{emf}$ and $\Phi_B'$, no conservation law, and no statement about singular sources; the transport identity is proved separately under its own hypotheses.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] A **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Adopt as physical postulates of this framework, on the spacetime and particle
model of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and
[[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] and on the special-relativity particle
model [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]:

(i) [Test charge in a prescribed external field] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a
constant charge parameter ([[def-em-sources]]), $m>0$ an externally supplied
rest mass, $x:J\to A$ a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline with
four-velocity $U$, and let $F$ be a prescribed field of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph
of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle. Adopt the equation of
motion

$$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),$$

where $\Phi$ is the raised-index operator of the field at the event $x(\tau)$,
defined by $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$
([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]); equivalently
$m\,dU^\mu/d\tau=q\,F^{\mu\nu}U_\nu$. Here $dU/d\tau$ is the derivative of $U$
with respect to proper time, that is, the four-acceleration of the worldline
([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). The particle's own field
is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no
self-force.

(ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of
[[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated
matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density
$\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit
W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the
spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local
interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed
current alone.

(iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within
electromagnetism. The coupling is adopted for constant $q$ and $m>0$; no
magnetic-monopole coupling, no radiation reaction and no self-force are
included. In particular the nonrelativistic coordinate statement
$mr''=q(E+r'\times B)$ is not adopted as exact: the adopted statement is the
covariant one of clause (i), and any low-speed statement requires its own
approximation hypotheses and error bounds.

derivations.claim: Fix $t\in J$. By [F1] the contact-model emf is the sum of the four segment integrals of $E+v_\gamma\times B$ with the segmentwise velocities. On the two rail portions and the left closing side the material velocity is zero and $E=0$, so the integrand vanishes identically and each of those three integrals is $0$. On the bar, parametrized by $s\mapsto(x(t),s,0)$ with $s$ from $-l/2$ to $l/2$ in the $+e_2$ direction, the velocity is $v_b=x'(t)e_1$, so [F2] gives $v_b\times B=x'(t)e_1\times B_0e_3=-B_0x'(t)e_2$ and [F3] gives $\langle v_b\times B,e_2\rangle=-B_0x'(t)$; the bar integral is therefore $\int_{-l/2}^{l/2}(-B_0x'(t))\,ds=-B_0lx'(t)$. Hence $\mathrm{emf}(t)=-B_0lx'(t)$ for every $t\in J$.

For the force let $j_t=(I(t)/A)e_2$ on the interior of $K_t$ and extend it by zero outside that interior, the difference with any boundary extension being confined to the null faces of $K_t$ by [F7]. By [F2] the force density is $j_t\times B_0e_3=(I(t)B_0/A)e_1$, a constant vector on the interior; hence, using [F4], [F5] and [F6] applied to the constant integrand and [F7] for the volume $\lambda_3(K_t)=dlh=Al$,
$$F(t)=\int_{K_t}j_t\times B\,d\lambda_3=\frac{I(t)B_0}{A}e_1\,\lambda_3(K_t)=I(t)B_0le_1 .$$
The integral is absolutely finite. This is the prescribed local matter coupling [F11] applied to the declared current density; it asserts no force on an arbitrary source without such a matter model.

The flux through the frozen rectangle $R(t)=[a_0,x(t)]\times[-l/2,l/2]\times\{0\}$ with normal $e_3$ is the surface integral of the constant field $B_0e_3$, that is $\Phi(t)=B_0\,\lambda_2(R(t))=B_0l(x(t)-a_0)$ with $\lambda_2$ the two-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the plane; by [F7] applied to the rectangle with sides $x(t)-a_0$ and $l$ this is the stated value (and it is $0$ when $x(t)=a_0$, where the rectangle is degenerate). Since $x$ is $C^1$ on $J$ with the prescribed neighbourhood extension, [F8] gives $\Phi'(t)=B_0lx'(t)$ on the interior of $J$ and one-sided at the endpoints of $J$, hence $\mathrm{emf}(t)=-\Phi'(t)$ by step 1.1; the magnitude is $B_0l|x'(t)|$ because $B_0\ge0$ and $l>0$.

The signed power balance is immediate from steps 1.1 and 1.2 and the Euclidean pairing: with $v_b=x'(t)e_1$ and $\langle e_1,e_1\rangle=1$ by [F3], $F(t)\cdot v_b(t)=I(t)B_0lx'(t)$ and $\mathrm{emf}(t)I(t)=-B_0lx'(t)I(t)$, so the sum is $0$ for every sign of $I(t)$ and of $x'(t)$, including the zero values.

The three displayed conclusions are established by steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2. The fields and units are those of [F9] and [F10]; the model is the hypothetical sliding-contact model of the Statement, not a single-valued smooth material sheet of [F12], and its strict theorem is not used; the laboratory reading is that of [F13]. No measurement, self-field, radiation, dissipative or dynamical conclusion is asserted, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used only through the explicitly cited box-measure and integral interfaces.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement fixes $l>0$, $a_0<a_1$, $d,h>0$ and a nonempty interval $J$; the four segment integrals are over nondegenerate or degenerate segments and $K_t$ is a nondegenerate box for every $t$, so no empty-family case arises and none is needed.

Step 2.1 covers $B_0=0$: then $\Phi\equiv0$ and step 1.1 gives $\mathrm{emf}\equiv0$, while step 1.2 gives $F\equiv0$ and step 2.2 the balance $0=0$ for every current. The case $x'\equiv0$ likewise gives $\mathrm{emf}\equiv0$ and zero mechanical power.
The model has a single bar; the degenerate rail portion at $x(t)=a_0$ is a single point whose line integral is 0 under the piecewise $C^1$ convention [F1], as step 1.1 uses.

If $x(t)=a_0$ the flux rectangle $R(t)$ has zero area and step 2.1 computes $\Phi=0$; the "flux" of a degenerate rectangle and the null faces of $K_t$ in [F7] are handled explicitly, and no normal-chart argument is required for them.

The prescribed motion $x$ carries the stated $C^1$ neighbourhood extension whenever $J$ is not open; step 2.1 differentiates $\Phi$ on the interior of $J$ and one-sidedly at included endpoints, and no derivative at contacts is used.

Countable Choice is used only through the box-measure and integral interfaces [F4]-[F7] of the bar-volume computation in step 1.2, as step 3.1 records; the emf and balance computations of steps 1.1 and 2.2 are finite and explicit.
No if-and-only-if claim is made; step 2.1 proves $\mathrm{emf}=-\Phi'$ as an identity for the declared model, and the magnitude statement is read from the sign of $B_0\ge0$ and $l>0$.

There is no converse direction: the Statement defines the contact-model emf by the segment integrals and proves only the identities (a)-(c); steps 1.1 and 2.1 never claim that an arbitrary emf or power balance determines the motion or the current.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $N$ be the Newtonian potential transform of [[def-newtonian-potential]] in dimension $n=3$: for a finite-valued function $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}f=\overline{\{x\in\mathbb R^3:f(x)\ne0\}}$ is compact ([[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]),
$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$$
at each $x\in\mathbb R^3$ where this integral is absolutely finite, where $\Phi$ is the normalized kernel of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]] with its value at the pole assigned $0$, so that $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$; write also $g(0):=0$ and $g(z):=|z|^{-1}$ for $z\ne0$, so that $\Phi=g/(4\pi)$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$. Let $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ be the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ be the set of maps each of whose three components is smooth ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with compact support in the above sense. For $u,v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ write $Nu:=(Nu_1,Nu_2,Nu_3)$ componentwise, so that the linkage pairing is the map
$$B(u,v):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle u(x),Nv(x)\rangle\,d\lambda_3(x).$$
Then all three integrals
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle u(x),Nv(x)\rangle\,d\lambda_3(x),\qquad\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle Nu(x),v(x)\rangle\,d\lambda_3(x),\qquad\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x)$$
converge absolutely ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]) and have the same value; therefore $B$ is well defined, real-valued, symmetric, $B(u,v)=B(v,u)$, and bilinear over $\mathbb R$ in each argument. In particular the common value of the three integrals is unchanged by exchanging the two density fields $u$ and $v$.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mu_0>0$ be a real scalar parameter, let $J\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $\operatorname{div}J=0$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]), and define componentwise
$$A:=\mu_0N(J),\qquad A_i=\mu_0\,N(J_i),\qquad N f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)}{4\pi|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y),$$
the Newtonian vector potential attached to [[def-newtonian-potential]] in dimension three. Then:

(a) $A\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}A=0$ and $-\Delta A=\mu_0J$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$, componentwise ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]);

(b) there is $C>0$ with $|\operatorname{curl}A(x)|\le C/(1+|x|^2)$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$; hence $\operatorname{curl}A\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $\langle A,J\rangle\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$, both in the ordinary Lebesgue sense ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]);

(c) the curl-field energy identity
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\operatorname{curl}A|^2\,d\lambda_3=\mu_0\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle A,J\rangle\,d\lambda_3$$
holds, and equivalently $\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle A,J\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\operatorname{curl}A|^2\,d\lambda_3\ge0$.

The identity is stated for the explicit smooth compact currents and the Newtonian construction; no uniqueness, no decay of $A$ itself beyond the curl bound of (b), and no extension to singular currents is claimed.

For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

**(a) [Steady-current regime].** A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields.

**(c1) [Closed thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution
$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

**(c2) [Infinite straight wire].** For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is
$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

**(c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet].** For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is
$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.

**(c4) [Admissibility].** A field $B$ is admitted for one of these declared models when: $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ (hence a distribution by [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $C^1$ off the support of the current; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ hold pointwise off that support; the distributional identities $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold against every scalar divergence test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and vector curl test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]; $B$ has the model's declared symmetry (invariance under translations along and rotations about the axis in (c2) and (c3); no symmetry is required in (c1)); and $B$ obeys the decay requirement: $|B(x)|\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in (c1), and in (c2), (c3) the supremum of $|B|$ over every compact set of cross-sectional parameters tends to $0$ as the transverse radius $\rho\to\infty$. The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

**(d) [Scope].** This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the equations in (c4) define a mathematical admissibility predicate; its physical adoption for these source objects is a separate postulate, and no product of distributions is formed.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. For a measurable compactly supported
$f$, define
$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$$
at each $x$ where the integral is absolutely finite. Whenever this integral
is finite almost everywhere, $Nf$ also denotes its almost-everywhere class.
The following items establish everywhere convergence for bounded compact data
and almost-everywhere convergence for compact $L^1$ data; the definition itself
makes no unconditional convergence claim.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F$, $\nabla\operatorname{div}F$ and $\Delta F$ are all defined on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F=\nabla\operatorname{div}F-\Delta F.$$

Here $\Delta F$ is the componentwise Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.
