At $t_0$: $w(t_0)=z_0$ gives $Q(t_0)=\operatorname{Re}z_0=Q_0$, and $w'(t_0)=\mathrm i\Omega z_0=\mathrm i\Omega Q_0+I_0$ gives $Q'(t_0)=I_0$. Euler's formula [F13] expands $\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(t-t_0))=\cos\Omega(t-t_0)+\mathrm i\sin\Omega(t-t_0)$, and multiplying out $w=z_0\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(t-t_0))$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=Q_0\cos\Omega(t-t_0)+(I_0/\Omega)\sin\Omega(t-t_0)$, with the real trigonometric functions of [F13] and the real restriction recorded in [F14]. For $J=\{t_0\}$ the same formulas are evaluated at $t_0$, the entire function supplying the jets $\dot Q(t_0)=I_0$ and $\ddot Q(t_0)=-\Omega^2Q_0=-Q_0/(LC)$ by the same computation, so the LC candidate needs no separate singleton convention.

(a) Along the solution of step 1.1 the function $t\mapsto\frac12LI(t)^2$ is differentiable at every interior point of $J$ (and one-sidedly at included endpoints) by [F5], with derivative $LI\dot I$; substituting the circuit equation $L\dot I=V-RI$ gives $LI\dot I=VI-RI^2$, which is the power identity.

(b) Define $E(t):=\frac12LQ'(t)^2+\frac{Q(t)^2}{2C}$; by [F6] and step 1.2 the functions $Q$ and $Q'$ are continuous, so $E$ is continuous on $J$, and at every interior point of $J$ the product and scalar rules of [F5] give $E'=LQ'Q''+QQ'/C=Q'(LQ''+Q/C)=0$ by the equation of step 1.2. By [F15], $E$ is constant on $J$, and its value is $E(t_0)=\frac12LI_0^2+\frac{Q_0^2}{2C}$ by the initial values of step 1.2. The first summand is the inductive bookkeeping energy of [F16], and for the optional geometric identification of the Statement the second summand is the frozen electrostatic field energy supplied by the declared clause of [L1] under full AC and the stated conductor arrangement, with $C=C_{11}$ and $V_1=Q/C_{11}$; the magnetic realization of the inductive term is the separate smooth-profile clause of [F16], under its $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ premise. For $J=\{t_0\}$ the constant-energy display is the value at $t_0$ supplied by step 1.2, so no derivative of a singleton restriction is used.

The full choice hypothesis of the geometric identification is [A1], and the inductive realization of [F16] carries the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [A2]; full AC yields it, because for a sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets the family $\{X_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ of its values consists of nonempty sets, so [A1] provides a choice function $g$ on that family and $n\mapsto g(X_n)$ is a choice function for the sequence, as [A2] requires. Hence clause (b) is available under its stated hypotheses, and the RL and LC algebra of steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2 is choice-free and uses neither [A1] nor [A2].

Clauses (a)-(c) are established: step 1.1 and step 2.1 give the existence, uniqueness, formula and power identity of (a); step 1.2 and step 2.2 give the solution, initial values, cosine-sine form, energy identity and conservation of (b), with the geometric identification delegated to [L1]; step 3.1 accounts for the choice use. The units are [F17]; no general network completeness, no full time-dependent Maxwell solution, no radiation or distributed-element effect and no empirical claim is asserted, and both statements are consequences of the expressly adopted relations of [F1].

boundaries.evidence: The hypothesis $t_0\in J$ excludes an empty interval; if $J=\{t_0\}$ the singleton clauses of steps 1.1 and 1.2 apply, and step 2.2 reads the constant energy at $t_0$.

For $R=0$ step 1.1 reduces the formula to $I_0+L^{-1}\int_{t_0}^tV$; for $I_0=0$ and $V\equiv0$ it gives $I\equiv0$ and the power identity $0=0$; for $Q_0=I_0=0$ step 1.2 gives $w\equiv0$ and step 2.2 gives $E\equiv0$.
No counting parameter occurs: the LC frequency is the single number $\Omega=(LC)^{-1/2}>0$ of step 1.2, fixed by the product $LC$ alone, and the RL coefficient is the single ratio $R/L$.

For $J=\{t_0\}$ step 1.1 gives the restriction $I_0$ and the canonical-extension jet $(V(t_0)-RI_0)/L$ without asserting a derivative of the singleton restriction, and step 1.2 gives the LC jets $\dot Q=I_0$, $\ddot Q=-Q_0/(LC)$ from the entire candidate.

For nondegenerate $J$ the derivatives are domain-relative with one-sided values at included endpoints in the sense of [F4], and step 1.1 applies [F3] on $J$; the open-neighbourhood extension of the Statement supplies the endpoint jets and step 2.2 differentiates only at interior points, as [F15] requires.

The RL solution, the LC candidate and the energy algebra of steps 1.1-2.2 are choice-free as the Statement declares; full AC enters only through [L1]'s geometric capacitor identification in step 2.2, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ only through [F16]'s smooth-profile realization, with step 3.1 deriving the latter from the former.
The item asserts no if-and-only-if of its own; the energy conservation of step 2.2 is an equality of functions, and the equivalence $U(I)=0\iff J_I=0$ used through [F16] is quoted from its supplier.
There is no converse direction to discharge: step 2.2 proves $E'\equiv0$ and hence constancy, and does not claim that constant energy forces the LC equation, which is separately verified in step 1.2.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the lumped circuit model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for clause (b), where it is inherited from the linkage suppliers.

(a) [Terminal-energy bookkeeping] Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]), let $t_0,t_1\in J$, let $L\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be constant and symmetric, let $I:J\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$ in the following sense: $I$ extends to a $C^1$ map on an open interval containing $J$, so that the derivatives used below are those of the extension (one-sided at included endpoints of $J$, and not intrinsic to a value restriction when $J$ is a singleton), and let $V(t):=L\dot I(t)$ be the terminal-voltage vector of the inductive branches as adopted in [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] (the Faraday branch: the terminal voltage of a branch is the rate of change of its flux linkage $\Phi=LI$). Then
$$\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle\,dt=\frac12\langle I(t_1),LI(t_1)\rangle-\frac12\langle I(t_0),LI(t_0)\rangle ,$$
and for $n=1$ with $L>0$ this reads $\int_{t_0}^{t_1}V I\,dt=\frac12L\bigl(I(t_1)^2-I(t_0)^2\bigr)$: the accumulated terminal energy equals the change of the inductor bookkeeping energy $\frac12LI^2$. The identity is exact for every such $C^1$ current and fixed geometry; it uses only symmetry of $L$, the product rule and the fundamental theorem of calculus. For a changing geometry the mechanical work done on the circuit is an additional term and is not covered here.

(b) [Identification with the frozen field energy] Suppose in addition that the currents are realized by fixed compact smooth conserved profiles $j_1,\dots,j_n$ of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), with instantaneous source $J(t):=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha(t)j_\alpha$, and that the inductance matrix is the linkage matrix of those profiles in the sense of [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]]: $L_{\alpha\beta}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\iint\frac{\langle j_\alpha(x),j_\beta(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x)$. Then for every $t\in J$
$$\frac12\langle I(t),LI(t)\rangle=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J(t),A_{J(t)}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J(t)}|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge0,$$
where $A_{J(t)}$ is the Coulomb-gauge Newtonian vector potential and $B_{J(t)}=\operatorname{curl}A_{J(t)}$ of that theorem: the right-hand side is the magnetic field energy of the frozen instantaneous configuration, and the accumulated terminal energy of (a) between $t_0$ and $t_1$ is the change of this field energy. The relation $V=L\dot I$ is the explicitly adopted terminal law of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; the identification of the model's inductance matrix with the smooth-profile linkage matrix is part of the adopted model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]].

(c) [Scope] no radiation, distributed-element, material-loss, moving-geometry or thin-wire self-inductance claim is made; the frozen-configuration energy is not asserted to be the energy of a time-dependent full Maxwell solution.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $j_1,\dots,j_n\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}j_\alpha=0$ be fixed compact smooth conserved current profiles of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. Fix amplitudes $I\in\mathbb R^n$, put $J_I:=\sum_{\alpha=1}^nI_\alpha j_\alpha$, let $A_{J_I}$ be the Coulomb-gauge Newtonian vector potential of [[pthm-em-magnetostatic-vector-potential]] applied to the conserved current $J_I$, and let $B_{J_I}=\operatorname{curl}A_{J_I}$. Define the linkage coefficients
$$L_{\alpha\beta}:=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\langle j_\alpha(x),j_\beta(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x),\qquad\alpha,\beta=1,\dots,n .$$
Then:

(a) [Finiteness and self-energy] every $L_{\alpha\beta}$ is a finite real number: the defining double integral converges absolutely, and in particular every self-coefficient $L_{\alpha\alpha}$ is finite, so the compact smooth profiles carry a finite self-energy. This is a statement about the smooth profiles only; no finite value is assigned to a zero-radius thin-wire self-inductance.

(b) [Reciprocity and flux linkage] $L_{\alpha\beta}=L_{\beta\alpha}$ for all $\alpha,\beta$; $A_{J_I}=\sum_{\alpha}I_\alpha A_{j_\alpha}$ componentwise; and for every $\beta$ the linkage integral is
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle j_\beta,A_{J_I}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\sum_{\alpha=1}^nL_{\beta\alpha}I_\alpha .$$
Thus the numbers $L_{\alpha\beta}$ are the linkage coefficients of the profiles: the linkage of profile $\beta$ with the field of the superposition is the linear combination $\sum_\alpha L_{\beta\alpha}I_\alpha$.

(c) [Magnetic energy and positivity] with $U(I):=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J_I,A_{J_I}\rangle\,d\lambda_3$,
$$U(I)=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^nL_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha I_\beta=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J_I}|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge0,$$
all quantities finite; moreover $U(I)=0$ holds precisely when $J_I=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$. Consequently the symmetric matrix $L=(L_{\alpha\beta})$ is positive semidefinite, and it is positive definite exactly when the profiles are pointwise linearly independent, i.e. when $\sum_\alpha I_\alpha j_\alpha\equiv0$ forces $I=0$.

(d) [Scope] the theorem concerns fixed compact smooth conserved current profiles and their Coulomb-gauge fields. It asserts no thin-wire, sheet or singular self-inductance; no time-dependent, moving, radiating or material configuration; and no uniqueness of the vector potential. The identification of these coefficients with the inductance matrix of the adopted lumped circuit model, and of the linkage derivatives with terminal voltages, is adopted in [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; the strict material-loop theorem applies separately only to an actual moving sheet and compatible smooth Maxwell fields satisfying its hypotheses. No terminal-voltage law for arbitrary varying frozen profiles is inferred from the present magnetostatic computation.

For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

**(a) [Steady-current regime].** A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields.

**(c1) [Closed thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution
$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

**(c2) [Infinite straight wire].** For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is
$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

**(c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet].** For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is
$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.

**(c4) [Admissibility].** A field $B$ is admitted for one of these declared models when: $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ (hence a distribution by [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $C^1$ off the support of the current; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ hold pointwise off that support; the distributional identities $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold against every scalar divergence test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and vector curl test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]; $B$ has the model's declared symmetry (invariance under translations along and rotations about the axis in (c2) and (c3); no symmetry is required in (c1)); and $B$ obeys the decay requirement: $|B(x)|\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in (c1), and in (c2), (c3) the supremum of $|B|$ over every compact set of cross-sectional parameters tends to $0$ as the transverse radius $\rho\to\infty$. The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

**(d) [Scope].** This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the equations in (c4) define a mathematical admissibility predicate; its physical adoption for these source objects is a separate postulate, and no product of distributions is formed.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Adopt as a modelling postulate of this framework the following reduced circuit description, to be used only within its declared regime. Let the laboratory region, its chart and units and the compact smooth current class be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-steady-current-regime]], and let the material response be one of the branches of [[post-em-material-closure]].

(a) [Circuit data] Fix a finite set of branches $\alpha=1,\dots,n$ (and capacitive branches $\beta=1,\dots,m$) and a time interval $J$. The model carries branch currents $I_\alpha:J\to\mathbb R$, branch charges $Q_\beta:J\to\mathbb R$, terminal potentials $V_\alpha:J\to\mathbb R$, and constant matrices $L\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ and $R\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, with $L$ and $C$ symmetric, $C$ positive definite and $R$ symmetric positive semidefinite. The matrices, the terminal geometry and the choice of independent loops are fixed data of the model; they are declared, not derived here, and the smooth compact-current realization of the inductive couplings and its reciprocity are analysed separately on this page.

(b) [Branch relations and network laws] In the declared regime the inductive branches obey the Faraday branch relation $V(t)=L\dot I(t)$, i.e. each terminal potential is the rate of change of the branch flux linkage $LI$; the capacitive branches obey $V=C^{-1}Q$ (in the scalar case $V_\beta=Q_\beta/C_{\beta\beta}$); the resistive branches obey $V=RI$, the circuit form of the Ohmic relation of [[post-em-material-closure]]; and the network laws are Kirchhoff's current law at each node and loop voltage balance around each independent loop. The circuit-level bookkeeping quantities of the model are the flux linkage $LI$ and the stored energies $\tfrac12I^{\mathsf T}LI$ and $\tfrac12Q^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}Q$.

(c) [Quasistatic regime declaration] The description is confined to configurations whose largest geometric extent $\ell$ and shortest time scale $T$ of interest satisfy the quasistatic smallness condition $\ell/(cT)\ll1$, with negligible radiation and negligible leakage and with specified conductor geometry and ideal terminals. The inequality is a declared regime of validity of the model; no error bound for an arbitrary full Maxwell solution follows from it alone, and the model does not assert that every asymptotically small configuration is described to any particular accuracy.

(d) [Status, units and scope] This is an adopted reduced model, not a deduction from the vacuum Maxwell equations; the matrices $L,C,R$ are model data, no microscopic constitutive law beyond the adopted branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] is asserted, and no radiation, distributed-element, nonlinear, hysteretic, leakage or proximity effect is included. SI units consistent with [[def-em-si-conventions]] are used: $V$ in volts, $I$ in amperes, $Q$ in coulombs, $t$ in seconds, $L$ in henries ($\mathrm H=\mathrm V\,\mathrm s\,\mathrm A^{-1}$), $C$ in farads ($\mathrm F=\mathrm C\,\mathrm V^{-1}$) and $R$ in ohms ($\Omega=\mathrm V\,\mathrm A^{-1}$). Where conductor matter moves, material speeds are subluminal, $|v|<c$, when the relativistic force interpretation is used.

derivations.claim: Clause (a): by [F5], $\frac12\langle I(t),LI(t)\rangle=\frac12L_1I_1^2+MI_1I_2+\frac12L_2I_2^2$, which is the displayed $W(t)$. Differentiating termwise with the product and scalar rules of [F6] gives $\dot W=L_1I_1\dot I_1+M(\dot I_1I_2+I_1\dot I_2)+L_2I_2\dot I_2=(L_1\dot I_1+M\dot I_2)I_1+(M\dot I_1+L_2\dot I_2)I_2=V_1I_1+V_2I_2$, since $[L\dot I]_\alpha=V_\alpha$; the sign reading of the mutual term is immediate from $W=\frac12L_1I_1^2+\frac12L_2I_2^2+MI_1I_2$ for $M>0$.

Clause (b): under the realization hypothesis, $W(t)=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha(t)I_\beta(t)=U(I(t))\ge0$ at each $t$ by [F3], the block $L$ being by hypothesis the linkage matrix of the two profiles. Substituting $I=(\sqrt{L_2},-\sqrt{L_1})$ gives $W=L_1L_2-M\sqrt{L_1L_2}\ge0$, that is $M\le\sqrt{L_1L_2}$; substituting $I=(\sqrt{L_2},+\sqrt{L_1})$ gives $W=L_1L_2+M\sqrt{L_1L_2}\ge0$, that is $M\ge-\sqrt{L_1L_2}$; together, $|M|\le\sqrt{L_1L_2}$. If $M=s\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ and $I=(\sqrt{L_2},-s\sqrt{L_1})$, the same expansion gives $W=L_1L_2-sM\sqrt{L_1L_2}=L_1L_2-L_1L_2=0$, so by the vanishing clause of [F3] the associated current $J_I$ vanishes pointwise.

Clause (c): with $N_1=\sqrt{L_1/\Lambda}$ and $N_2=\sqrt{L_2/\Lambda}$ one has $L_1=\Lambda N_1^2$, $L_2=\Lambda N_2^2$ and $M=\sqrt{L_1L_2}=\Lambda N_1N_2$ because $N_1N_2=\sqrt{L_1L_2}/\Lambda$. Hence, using $V_\alpha=\sum_\beta L_{\alpha\beta}\dot I_\beta$, $V_1=L_1\dot I_1+M\dot I_2=\Lambda N_1(N_1\dot I_1+N_2\dot I_2)=N_1\dot\Phi_c$ and $V_2=M\dot I_1+L_2\dot I_2=\Lambda N_2(N_1\dot I_1+N_2\dot I_2)=N_2\dot\Phi_c$ with $\Phi_c=\Lambda(N_1I_1+N_2I_2)$; dividing by $N_1,N_2>0$ gives the common ratio, and $e_\alpha=-V_\alpha$ reverses the common sign. For the energy, $W=\frac12L_1I_1^2+MI_1I_2+\frac12L_2I_2^2=\frac12\Lambda(N_1I_1+N_2I_2)^2=\Phi_c^2/(2\Lambda)$ by the displayed relations and the binomial expansion.

Clause (d), strict-linkage non-identity: suppose $|M|<\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ and $V_2=kV_1$ held for all $C^1$ currents on $J$; then $\sum_\beta L_{2\beta}\dot I_\beta=k\sum_\beta L_{1\beta}\dot I_\beta$ for every such current. Fix any point $t_0\in J$ (any point when $J$ is a singleton) and, for each vector $a=(a_1,a_2)\in\mathbb R^2$, take the affine history $I(t)=c+(t-t_0)a$ (any fixed $c\in\mathbb R^2$) on $J$, which is the restriction of the affine map of $t$ on $\mathbb R$ and hence carries the stated $C^1$ open-neighbourhood extension with $\dot I\equiv a$; substituting gives $(L_{21}-kL_{11})a_1+(L_{22}-kL_{12})a_2=0$ for all $a$, hence $L_{21}=kL_{11}$ and $L_{22}=kL_{12}$, i.e. $\operatorname{row}_2L=k\operatorname{row}_1L$. Then $L_1k=M$ and $L_2=kM=M^2/L_1$, so $L_1L_2-M^2=0$, contradicting $L_1L_2-M^2>0$ from $|M|<\sqrt{L_1L_2}$; hence no such $k$ makes the ratio a universal identity. Accidental satisfaction occurs: any history with $\dot I$ in the kernel of the nonzero functional $a\mapsto(L_{21}-kL_{11})a_1+(L_{22}-kL_{12})a_2$ satisfies $V_2=kV_1$ at every time, that kernel being nontrivial because one linear equation in two unknowns always has a nonzero solution; in particular the constant currents give $V_1=V_2=0$. For the reversed winding with $M=s\sqrt{L_1L_2}$, put $\Phi_c=\Lambda(N_1I_1+sN_2I_2)$; then $V_1=L_1\dot I_1+M\dot I_2=\Lambda N_1(N_1\dot I_1+sN_2\dot I_2)=N_1\dot\Phi_c$ and $V_2=M\dot I_1+L_2\dot I_2=\Lambda sN_2(N_1\dot I_1+sN_2\dot I_2)=sN_2\dot\Phi_c$ because $s^2=1$, so $V_1/N_1=V_2/(sN_2)=\dot\Phi_c$, and $W=\frac12\Lambda(N_1I_1+sN_2I_2)^2=\Phi_c^2/(2\Lambda)$.

Steps 1.1-1.4 establish (a)-(d): steps 1.1-1.2 give (a) and the bound and null-direction clauses of (b), and steps 1.3-1.4 give the common-flux model (c) and the limitations (d). The computation is conditional on the adopted lumped model [F1], its units are [F7], and no leakage, loss, material or measurement claim is added; the terminal-voltage jets on a singleton interval are those of the specified extension. Countable Choice is used only through the realization clause (b), via [F3]; the algebraic clauses (a), (c) and (d) are choice-free.

boundaries.evidence: The block has the fixed size $2$ and $L_1,L_2>0$; the algebra of steps 1.1-1.4 needs no nonemptiness beyond these hypotheses, and the zero-current case is covered separately.

For $I_1=I_2=0$ step 1.1 gives $W=0$ and $V_1=V_2=0$; step 1.4's kernel description includes the constant (hence zero-derivative) histories, and the common-flux relations of step 1.3 degenerate to $\Phi_c=0$ with $W=0$.
The turns ratio is fixed by the model data: $N_1=N_2=1$ when $L_1=L_2=\Lambda$, as step 1.3 displays, and no other counting parameter occurs.

At perfect linkage the null direction $I=(\sqrt{L_2},-s\sqrt{L_1})$ is a genuinely nonzero current vector, so step 1.2 exhibits a nontrivial kernel of $L$; under strict linkage step 1.4 uses $L_1L_2-M^2>0$, i.e. positive definiteness, and the contradiction follows from the forced vanishing of that determinant.
The interval $J$ may be non-open; the stated $C^1$ open-neighbourhood extension of the currents supplies the derivatives used in steps 1.1-1.4, and no separate endpoint claim is made.
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used only through the realization clause (b) via [F3] in step 1.2; the algebraic clauses (a), (c) and (d) of steps 1.1, 1.3 and 1.4 are choice-free, as step 2.1 records.
No if-and-only-if claim is made; the vanishing clause used in step 1.2 is the quoted equivalence of [F3], and the item proves equalities (the bound, the ratio, the energy) rather than equivalences.

There is no converse direction; step 1.4 proves a negative statement (failure of a universal voltage ratio) by contradiction and exhibits accidental histories satisfying the ratio without claiming that they realise the ideal model.

citations.quote:
Assume the lumped circuit model and its units as in [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]) and let $t_0\in J$. For a nondegenerate $J$, derivatives are domain-relative, with one-sided values at included endpoints, in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; the functions constructed below also admit the stated $C^k$ open-neighbourhood extensions. If $J=\{t_0\}$, the formulas specify the initial values and the jets of the explicitly constructed extensions below, rather than an intrinsic derivative of a singleton restriction. The RL solution, the LC candidate and the bookkeeping-energy algebra use no choice principle. Only the optional geometric capacitor identification in (b) assumes full Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and its $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ consequence ([[def-countable-choice]]), exactly as [[pthm-em-capacitance-energy]] requires. The inductive energy is that of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]].

(a) [RL circuit] Let $L>0$ and $R\ge0$ be constants and let $V:J\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Then the initial value problem
$$L\dot I(t)+R\,I(t)=V(t),\qquad I(t_0)=I_0\in\mathbb R,$$
has exactly one $C^1$ solution on every nondegenerate $J$, namely
$$I(t)=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\Bigr)\Bigl[I_0+\frac1L\int_{t_0}^{t}\exp\!\Bigl(\frac{R(s-t_0)}{L}\Bigr)V(s)\,ds\Bigr],$$
and along it the inductive bookkeeping energy satisfies the power identity
$$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\Bigl(\frac12LI(t)^2\Bigr)=L\dot I(t)I(t)=V(t)I(t)-R\,I(t)^2 ,$$
i.e. the terminal power splits into the rate of change of the inductive energy and the Ohmic term $RI^2$. (For $R=0$ the same formula reduces to $I=I_0+L^{-1}\int_{t_0}^tV$.) For $J=\{t_0\}$ its unique restriction is $I(t_0)=I_0$; the canonical extension obtained using the constant source $V(t_0)$ has jet $\dot I(t_0)=(V(t_0)-RI_0)/L$ and satisfies the same power algebra. No uniqueness of arbitrary extension germs is asserted.

(b) [LC oscillation] Let $L>0$, $C>0$ and set $\Omega:=(LC)^{-1/2}>0$, $z_0:=Q_0-\mathrm i\,I_0/\Omega$, $w(t):=z_0\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(t-t_0))$ with the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]], and $Q(t):=\operatorname{Re}w(t)$. Then $Q$ is of class $C^2$ on $J$, $Q(t_0)=Q_0$, $Q'(t_0)=I_0$, and
$$L\,Q''(t)+\frac{Q(t)}{C}=0\qquad\text{on }J ;$$
equivalently, with the real trigonometric functions of [[thm-eulers-formula]],
$$Q(t)=Q_0\cos\bigl(\Omega(t-t_0)\bigr)+\frac{I_0}{\Omega}\sin\bigl(\Omega(t-t_0)\bigr).$$
Moreover the total bookkeeping energy
$$E(t):=\frac12L\,Q'(t)^2+\frac{Q(t)^2}{2C}$$
satisfies $E'(t)=Q'(t)\bigl(LQ''(t)+Q(t)/C\bigr)=0$ on $J$, hence $E$ is constant with value $\frac12LI_0^2+\frac{Q_0^2}{2C}$: the two terms are the adopted capacitive and inductive bookkeeping energies, the latter as in [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]](a), so in the lossless loop their sum is conserved. For the additional geometric identification, explicitly choose the fixed compact separated conductor arrangement of [[pthm-em-capacitance-energy]] with bounded smooth ambient domain, connected vacuum, grounded outer boundary, zero volume source and its unit-Dirichlet solutions; drive only conductor 1 and ground the others, set the circuit parameter $C$ equal to that arrangement's $C_{11}>0$, and at each time set $V_1=Q/C_{11}$. Under full AC that supplier gives the frozen electrostatic field energy $Q^2/(2C_{11})$. An arbitrary declared $C>0$ is model data and is not automatically the capacitance of a particular arrangement. Any magnetic field-energy identification likewise requires the extra smooth-profile linkage realization of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]](b), under its $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis. Neither frozen realization is an asserted time-dependent full Maxwell solution. At a singleton time the entire LC candidate supplies the jets $\dot Q=I_0$, $\ddot Q=-Q_0/(LC)$ and the same constant energy.

(c) [Scope] both statements are consequences of the expressly adopted circuit reduction, with the sign conventions and relations of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; they assert no general network completeness, no derivation from the full time-dependent Maxwell system, no radiation or distributed-element effect and no empirical claim.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: Define the candidate $\varphi(t):=\frac{V_0}{R}+\left(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)$ on $J$. The function $t\mapsto-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}$ is affine with derivative $-\frac RL$ by [F3], and $\exp'=\exp$ by [F2], so the chain rule [F4] gives $\varphi'(t)=\left(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)\left(-\frac RL\right)\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)=-\frac RL\left(\varphi(t)-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)$. Therefore $L\varphi'(t)+R\varphi(t)=-R\left(\varphi(t)-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)+R\varphi(t)=V_0$ identically, and $\varphi(t_0)=\frac{V_0}{R}+\left(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)=I_0$.

Stationary solutions: if $I\equiv c$ is constant, then $L\dot I+RI=Rc$, so the equation $L\dot I+RI=V_0$ holds exactly when $c=V_0/R$; since $R>0$ there is exactly one such constant, namely $I\equiv V_0/R$.

Limit statement: if $J$ is unbounded above, then for $t\in J\cap[t_0,+\infty)$ the argument $-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}$ satisfies $-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\to-\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$ because $R/L>0$, so [F5] gives $\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)\to0$ and hence $I(t)\to V_0/R$ along that ray; the time constant is $\tau:=L/R$, so the decay factor is $\exp(-(t-t_0)/\tau)$.

Deviation identity: subtracting $V_0/R$ from the displayed formula gives $I(t)-V_0/R=\left(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)$; since $\exp(x)>0$ for real $x$ by [F6], taking absolute values preserves the exponential factor, so $|I(t)-V_0/R|=\left|I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right|\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)$ for every $t\in J$.
